pages.name: Lift the load
pages.text: A force does [[work]] when it moves something: force × the distance moved along it. That is the area under a force-distance graph. One joule is one newton moved through one metre. A winch lifts a 500 kg load at a steady speed. So the rope pulls with its weight, 500 × 9.81 = 4905 N. Over 10 m that is 4905 × 10 = 49,050 J, or 49.05 kJ. It is stored in the raised load as [[potential energy]], weight × height. The graph shows the stored energy rising in a straight line.

pages.name: Pull at an angle
pages.task: A rope pulls a crate 5 m along the floor. It pulls with 200 N, at 30° to the floor. How much work does the pull do?
pages.why: Only the part of the pull along the movement does work. Along the floor that part is 200 × cos 30° = 173.2 N. So the work is 173.2 × 5 = 866 J. The upward part, 100 N, moves nothing upwards, so it does no work.

pages.name: Power
pages.text: [[Power]] is how fast work is done. One joule each second is one watt. At 0.2 m/s the 10 m lift takes 50 s. So the power into the load is 49,050 ÷ 50 = 981 W. A steady pull gives a shortcut. Each second the load rises 0.2 m, so the rope does 4905 × 0.2 = 981 J. So power = force × speed. On the graph, power is the slope. A faster lift draws a steeper line up to the same energy.

pages.name: Power from work
pages.task: A winch lifts 200 kg through 5 m in 20 s. What power goes into the load?
pages.why: The weight is 200 × 9.81 = 1962 N. The work is 1962 × 5 = 9810 J. It takes 20 s, so the power is 9810 ÷ 20 = 490.5 W. Force × speed agrees: 1962 × 0.25 = 490.5 W.

pages.name: Same lift, half speed
pages.text: Same lift at half the speed: the same energy at half the power. At 0.1 m/s the force is still the load's weight. The height is still 10 m. So the work is the same 49.05 kJ. The time doubles to 100 s, so the power halves. The bars are half as long: 490.5 W into the load. The efficiency is held at 80% here, so the supply gives 613 W. A real motor's efficiency changes at half speed. Work says how much energy moves. Power says how fast.

pages.name: Losses and efficiency
pages.text: [[Efficiency]] is the fraction of the power in that reaches the load: useful power out ÷ power in. The motor draws electrical power from the supply. For a DC motor that is volts × amps. Some of it is lost as heat on the way. Say this winch is 80% efficient. To put 981 W into the load, it draws 981 ÷ 0.8 = 1226 W. The other 245 W becomes heat.

pages.task: A winch draws 800 W and puts 600 W into its load. How efficient is it?
pages.why: Efficiency is useful power out ÷ power in. That is 600 ÷ 800 = 0.75, or 75%. The other 200 W is lost as heat. Energy is never made, so no machine passes 100%.

pages.name: Brake off
pages.text: With the brake off, stored energy turns into speed. The load falls freely, with the drum and motor's spin left out. The picture stops it after 1 m. By then the 500 kg load's weight has done 4905 × 1 = 4905 J of work. That is now [[kinetic energy]], ½ × mass × speed². F = ma and v² = 2as give F × s = ½mv². The total stays the same: mgh = ½mv². The mass cancels, so any free-falling load reaches √(2 × 9.81 × 1) = 4.43 m/s. Heavier loads store more energy but reach the same speed.

pages.name: A chain block
pages.text: A chain block lifts by hand. Pull 30 m of hand chain with 250 N and a 500 kg load rises 1 m. Work in: 250 × 30 = 7500 J. Work out: 4905 × 1 = 4905 J. So it is 4905 ÷ 7500 = 65.4% efficient. Friction takes the other 2595 J. Load ÷ effort is its [[mechanical advantage]], 4905 ÷ 250 = 19.62. Chain pulled ÷ load lift is its [[velocity ratio]], 30. Efficiency, (load × lift) ÷ (effort × chain), regroups as (load ÷ effort) ÷ (chain ÷ lift). So 19.62 ÷ 30 is the same 65.4%.

pages.name: Another chain block
pages.task: On another chain block, 200 N on the hand chain raises a 250 kg load. 20 m of chain lifts it 1 m. How efficient is it?
pages.why: The load's weight is 250 × 9.81 = 2452.5 N. The mechanical advantage is 2452.5 ÷ 200 = 12.26. The velocity ratio is 20 ÷ 1 = 20. So the efficiency is 12.26 ÷ 20 = 61.3%.

pages.name: Power at the load
pages.task: A 500 kg load rises steadily at 0.2 m/s. What power goes into it?
pages.why: At a steady speed the rope pulls with the load's weight, 500 × 9.81 = 4905 N. Power = force × speed = 4905 × 0.2 = 981 W. All of it goes into height, as the speed does not change.

pages.name: The seized bolt
pages.task: A spanner puts a moment of 50 N m on a seized bolt. The bolt does not turn. How much work is done on the bolt?
pages.why: Work is force × the distance moved along the force. The bolt does not turn, so nothing moves. So no work is done: 0 J. The 50 N m is a moment, a turning effect. It shares the newton metre, but it is not energy.
